--- title: "The exercise" subtitle: "Extended course – Housing and racial bias" bibliography: [../../references.bib, ../../references-new.bib] --- This page sets out what you do in the Extended course on the Housing and racial bias case study, and where. The [background page](../../cases/housing/index.qmd) presents the original study, the SCORE replication and the five reanalyses of the robustness study of SCORE [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], and it is the place to start if you have not read it. The first day teaches R, the IDE and Quarto in the workspace of the case study, which you download and open in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), as the [Setup page](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html) describes. The second day is the one-day workshop, which takes all five tasks, and you do them in the workspace. The deck of that day shows each step with its output, so that you can compare your numbers with the slides. If your installation fails, the deck, whose slides run R inside your browser, and the [browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd), a page of this site that holds the same tasks, carry the work instead and give the same numbers. On the third day the analysis that you declared in Task 5 becomes a report of your own, written in Quarto in the workspace and kept under Git. --- ## The claim Five independent analysts reanalysed one claim of the original authors (OAs) in the robustness study [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. The claim, as the analysts received it, was: > "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" (p. 100 of the published article) The published result behind it is the coefficient of the Hispanic names in a logistic regression of a named greeting on the three groups of names, with community controls and the Hard Email indicator: **−0.82 (standard error 0.22) on 549 replies**, which the OAs translate into a gap of **−20.0 percentage points** in the probability of a named greeting, with a 95% confidence interval from −30.5 to −10.0. The data come from an experiment: 1,014 emails to housing authorities, each of which was signed with one of six names that were assigned at random. Your first job is to reproduce the value recorded in the robustness study for one of the analysts, whichever you choose, from the public file of the OAs. Your second is to depart from it deliberately, with a written reason, and to find out what that does to the estimate. ## The five analysts {#the-five-analysts} ::: {#tbl-five .cell tbl-cap='The five reanalyses, with the statistic recorded in the robustness study and the gap in percentage points by the course refit. Source: `cases/housing/data/analysts5.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Analyst Comparison Emails counted Recorded statistic Gap (points) Conclusion in Task 1
8PTRZ Hispanic against other names replies χ2 = 14.265 −17.3 evidence for the claim
UYV3F Hispanic against white names replies z = −3.771 −20.0 evidence for the claim
EWFMI Hispanic against white names (three-group model) replies z = 3.645 −19.4 evidence for the claim
25N5D Hispanic against white names all delivered emails χ2 = 13.683 −13.2 no evidence either way
P9W8Y three groups replies none recorded −20.0 no evidence either way
``` ::: ::: All five found Hispanic names greeted by name less often than the comparison names, and all four recorded statistics reproduce exactly on the public file. Two of the five nevertheless concluded in Task 1 of the robustness study that the data showed no evidence either way. The analysts compared different groups, counted different emails and used four kinds of test, and the [background page](../../cases/housing/index.qmd#sec-reanalysts) sets out what question each of them answered. --- ## The tasks The exercise runs as five numbered tasks. Each says what to do in the workspace and, where it differs, in the deck and the browser lab. ### Task 1 – The setup check The only aim is to reach the point where a line of R runs and the data are in front of you. *Workspace:* open the workspace folder in your IDE and run `source("R/check_setup.R")`, which prints OK when everything is in place and otherwise says what is missing. *Deck and browser lab:* wait for the engine to finish downloading, then run the setup cell. If your installation will not cooperate, carry on in the deck or in the [browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-1-setup), which run every later task. ### Task 2 – The data, the estimand and the graph First, meet the 1,014 emails of `housing_emails.csv` ([codebook](../../cases/housing/data/housing_emails_codebook.md)): who was emailed, which names they received, and what came back. Count the emails that bounced, the replies, and the replies that opened with the name of the sender, for each name. Second, write the **estimand statement** behind the claim. It says which comparison is made (Hispanic names against which names), which emails are counted (the replies, or every delivered email), and which outcome is compared. The [specification menu](../../cases/housing/menu.qmd) gives the template. Third, finish the **causal graph**. The name affects whether an official replies, and the reply comes before any greeting. Characteristics of the official that the data do not record, such as workload or habits of writing, affect both whether the official replies and whether a reply opens with a name, and so do characteristics of the community. The graph shows why comparing greetings among the replies conditions on a consequence of the name: it compares only the emails that an official chose to answer, and the name may itself have changed that choice, which the [background page](../../cases/housing/index.qmd#sec-posttreatment) calls post-treatment conditioning. It also shows why counting every delivered email keeps the comparison as randomisation made it. In the workspace, dagitty, the R package for causal graphs, answers the questions put to the graph, and tinyplot draws it. The deck and the browser lab cannot run dagitty, so they print the answers that dagitty gives for the graph with and without the arrow from the name to the greeting, read from a table that the course computed with dagitty. ### Task 3 – The reproduction Choose one of the five analysts in the table above and reproduce the analysis from the public file of the OAs, `housing_original.csv` ([codebook](../../cases/housing/data/housing_original_codebook.md)). Four of them have a statistic recorded in the robustness study, from the $\chi^2$ test of a two-by-two table that 8PTRZ ran to the logistic regression of three groups with covariates that EWFMI fitted, and all four come out exactly. The robustness study recorded no statistic for P9W8Y, so its likelihood-ratio test of the three groups, $\chi^2$ = 15.951 on 2 degrees of freedom, can be run again but cannot be matched against the record. The workspace has all five in its report and in `prep/reproduce_reanalyses.R`, and the deck and the [browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-3-reproduction) have a few cells for each analyst, one step each. In the workshop, when the facilitator says so, the whole class types the analyst and the value that each person reproduced, and sends them at the same moment. Then find out why your number is what it is. `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` apply a continuity correction to a two-by-two table unless they are told otherwise, so `correct = FALSE` gives 14.95 instead of 14.265 for 8PTRZ and 14.33 instead of 13.683 for 25N5D. The z of EWFMI is positive, where that of UYV3F is negative, because its model takes the Hispanic names as the base group. A reproduction depends on the defaults and the codings of the software as well as on the data and the model. ### Task 4 – The menu This task is **exploratory**. `try_spec()` takes the five arguments of the curve, `comparison`, `population`, `uncoded`, `model` and `adjust`, each of which defaults to the reference specification, so changing one thing means changing one argument. Try several specifications from the [specification menu](../../cases/housing/menu.qmd), one decision at a time, and note which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. An option that is not on the curve, such as `model = "three_group"`, is refused with the reason given in `menu_options.csv`. `my_experiments()` prints everything you have tried side by side. Then choose the one that you would defend, and `submit_exploration()` sends it to the class chart on the [Class results](../../cases/housing/class-results.qmd) page, where it appears as an open circle. Nothing in this task is preregistered. You may look, change your mind and try again, and the chart marks the result as exploratory for that reason. ### Task 5 – Declaration and report Choose **one** specification, one option for each decision, and complete the preregistration block **before you run it**: the claim, your option for each decision, and a sentence, grounded in your causal graph, on why the specification answers the claim. `prereg()` prints the block. `run_spec()` fits the specification that you declared, and `report_result()` sends the declared result to the class chart, where it appears as a filled circle. Then find where your result sits on the curve of 64 specifications. Task 4 and Task 5 run the same code. An exploratory specification can have been chosen because of its result and a declared one cannot, and you submit both so that the two sets of class results can be compared. ### Your report On the third day you turn the folder of the workspace into a repository, with the preregistration block that you completed in Task 5 as the first commit, and write the report around the declared analysis: the result with its uncertainty, its place on the curve of the claim, any departure from the declaration and the reason for it, and what the replication with new data adds. The page of [day 3](day-3.qmd) holds the steps. --- ## What counts as a result A result counts for the class chart if it is one of the 64 specifications on the curve, if it reaches the chart through `submit_exploration()` or `report_result()`, which fill in the class-results form for you, and if it comes with a written reason for each choice; two sentences are enough. The reasons are what make a set of different results more than a spread of numbers, because they show which differences between results come from different questions and which from different ways of answering the same one. --- ## Links The tools of the course: - [Slides of the workshop](../housing-one-day/slides.qmd) – the deck of the second day, which shows each step with its output; the pages of the first and the third days link the deck of each session. - [Setup](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html) – installing R and an IDE, and downloading the workspace. - [Setup help](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/help.html) – the problems that other participants have met, and what to do about each. - [The workspace](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing-workspace/) – the report of the workspace as it renders, with the output of every chunk under its code. - [Browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd) – the whole exercise and its data in a browser tab. - [Cheatsheet](../../cases/housing/cheatsheet.qmd) – the addresses, the helpers, the reproductions of Task 3 and the quick fixes of the second day on one page. The pages of the case study: - [Background](../../cases/housing/index.qmd) – the original study, the robustness study, the five reanalyses and the replication. - [Specification menu](../../cases/housing/menu.qmd) – the decisions of the analysis in three groups, with the options that the curve keeps and the reasons for the ones that it does not. - [Decision map](../../cases/housing/menu.qmd#map) – every decision in the order in which an analyst meets it; selecting an option rewrites the estimand statement and shows the result. - [Specification curve](../../cases/housing/curve.qmd) – the curve of 64 specifications, with the published result, the five reanalyses and the replication placed on it. - [Class results](../../cases/housing/class-results.qmd) – the live class chart.
